content.title: About
content.content: Tomatoes are the edible fruits of the tomato plant (Solanum lycopersicum), native to South America. They have a juicy, slightly sweet‑tart flavor and a characteristic bright red color. Raw tomatoes are eaten fresh and are also used in salads, sauces, soups, and many other dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tomatoes belong to the nightshade family and are botanically classified as berries, though they are culinarily treated as vegetables.
The heaviest recorded tomato weighed over 3.5 kg.
Lycopene gives tomatoes their red hue and acts as a powerful antioxidant.
There are more than 10,000 tomato varieties, differing in shape, size, taste, and color.
Tomatoes were first cultivated by the Aztecs and spread worldwide after the Columbian exchange.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Tomatoes provide a high amount of vitamin C, which supports the immune system and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains lycopene
items.content: Lycopene is a potent antioxidant that may reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease and certain cancers.

items.title: Good source of potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate blood pressure and supports proper heart function.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: Tomatoes are low in calories but high in water and fiber, promoting satiety.

items.title: Provides vitamin K1
items.content: Vitamin K1 is important for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to tomatoes, such as skin itching or swelling.

items.title: Solanine content
items.content: Unripe (green) tomatoes contain solanine, which can be toxic in large amounts; they should be avoided or cooked.

items.title: Food interactions
items.content: Tomatoes may enhance the effect of certain blood thinners due to their vitamin K content.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Raw tomatoes can be sliced for salads, sandwiches, or enjoyed as a snack with a pinch of salt and olive oil. They are also diced for salsa, added to pasta sauces, soups, and casseroles. For optimal flavor, let sliced tomatoes sit for a few minutes after seasoning.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store tomatoes at room temperature, away from direct sunlight, to allow them to ripen. Once fully ripe, they can be placed in the refrigerator for a few days, though this may affect texture. Avoid airtight containers, which can trap moisture and cause spoilage.
